_version.redaction_note: Public sources only, by direction. No assessed capability beyond what is openly published, no named objects, no watchlist membership, and no attribution of a specific platform to a specific operator. Archetypes are classes of thing, described by what they are built to do and how that shows up in observable behaviour.

_why_this_file_exists: The red team found the largest gap in the package: an operator had the physics, the procedure and the pattern of life, and no framework at all for what kind of thing was doing this or what it is for. Intent cannot be assessed without that. It is also why so many released reports describe precisely and assess not at all, because the analyst has nothing to reason from. Every report carries a mission paragraph; until now nothing in the package taught what goes in it.
_how_to_use: This is reference knowledge, not a lookup table for identifying objects. The trained skill is reasoning from observed behaviour to a plausible platform class, and from platform class to what the behaviour probably means. Operators should be able to say what a class can and cannot do, because the cannot is what rules hypotheses out.

archetypes.name: Belt collection platform
archetypes.built_to: Sit near a communications satellite and collect its signals, in the main beam or on a side lobe, potentially geolocating the ground emitter as well.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Drifts along the belt, stops, and holds a standoff from a target for an extended period. Plane matching is common. Moves on to the next target after weeks or months.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Long dwell, small station-keeping burns to hold the standoff, occasional larger burns to relocate. Behaviour is patient rather than aggressive.
can: Hold position near a target for months
Plane match to remain co-located cheaply
Relocate along the belt between targets
cannot: Do anything to the target physically
Approach to contact
archetypes.presence_implies: Signals collection against whatever it is parked near. The target is the object it is holding station on, and the interesting question is what that object transmits.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: Physical threat. A collection platform holding a standoff is doing exactly what it is for, and that is not an escalation.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Stable curve while holding. Changes at relocation or if it reorients for collection.

confusable_with.discriminator: A collector holds a standoff and stays. An inspector closes, circumnavigates and leaves. Dwell time and whether the geometry is being actively shaped are the tells.

archetypes.name: Inspector platform
archetypes.built_to: Approach another object closely enough to image it and characterise its payload, then withdraw.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Drifts, closes, circumnavigates naturally or under power, and departs. Often operates as a pair, and often loiters above or below the belt so it can drift past many objects.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Continuous slow drift with periodic close approaches, or a deliberate ingress and circumnavigation followed by departure. Approaches are close but transient by design.
can: Image a target at close range
Characterise external configuration and identify payload apertures
Repeat against many targets over time
cannot: Interfere with the target physically
Remain indefinitely without fuel cost
archetypes.presence_implies: Reconnaissance. Someone wants to know what a specific object looks like, which usually precedes something rather than being an end in itself.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: Imminent action. Inspection is a normal and frequent activity, and most inspections are followed by nothing.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Changes at reorientation for imaging, and during approach as the aspect angle changes.

confusable_with.discriminator: Inspection is transient and involves closing; collection is sustained and involves holding.

archetypes.name: Servicing and docking vehicle
archetypes.built_to: Rendezvous with another spacecraft and make physical contact, to refuel, extend life, relocate, or repair.
archetypes.orbital_signature: A deliberate, staged approach: plane match, phasing, shape and alignment, then a slow final closure over hours. Docking produces a merged signature and, afterwards, the pair manoeuvres as one body.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Patient and precise. Large delta-v to reach the target's plane, then very small burns during terminal approach. Post-docking manoeuvres are large because the combined mass is being moved.
can: Make physical contact with a cooperative or uncooperative object
Relocate an object it has captured
Extend the life of a target it is servicing
cannot: Be distinguished from a co-orbital weapon by geometry alone, which is the central problem it poses
archetypes.presence_implies: Capability for physical interaction. Whether that is servicing or something else is a question of intent, not of observation, and the honest report says so.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: Hostility. The same approach profile serves refuelling and capture, and this is the clearest case in the whole domain where capability and intent must be reported separately.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Merged signature after contact, often brighter than either object alone. Cross-tagging is expected below a few kilometres.

confusable_with.discriminator: There is no reliable geometric discriminator. Report the observation, report the capability, and state that intent is not observable. This is the single most important honest limitation in the package.

archetypes.name: Sub-satellite deployer
archetypes.built_to: Carry and release one or more smaller objects, which then operate independently.
archetypes.orbital_signature: A parent that produces a new catalogued object, often co-timed with a parent manoeuvre. The child then becomes the active party, manoeuvring while the parent holds.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Deployment may occur early in mission or very late. The child conducts proximity operations with the parent or with third objects, sometimes sustained for months, sometimes going quiet afterwards.
can: Release additional objects at a time of choosing
Present a headcount that changes without warning
Use the child as the manoeuvring vehicle while the parent stays clean
cannot: Recall a released object easily, though recapture has been demonstrated in some programmes
archetypes.presence_implies: The headcount is not fixed. An object of this class should be assumed capable of producing another at any point.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: That every new object is a weapon. Sub-satellites serve inspection, communication relay and technology demonstration.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: A step change in brightness at deployment as the configuration changes.

confusable_with.discriminator: Intent. A deployment is co-timed with a manoeuvre, produces a stable object, and the child usually manoeuvres afterwards. A breakup produces many objects, none of which manoeuvre.

archetypes.name: Ground-launched interceptor
archetypes.built_to: Reach an orbiting object on a ballistic trajectory and destroy it by collision.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Not an orbit. A suborbital ascent to an apogee at or near the target altitude, with a short flight for low-altitude targets and several hours for high-altitude ones.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Ascent, coast, possible trajectory adjustment and separation of a kill vehicle in the final hour, then terminal intercept. May receive updates from the ground during ascent.
can: Reach targets across a wide altitude band
Be launched from mobile ground equipment with little warning
Be retargeted during ascent
cannot: Loiter
Change target once committed to a final intercept path, having limited divert
Engage without adequate seeker lighting, assuming an electro-optical seeker
archetypes.presence_implies: A committed act. Unlike every other archetype here, this one has no benign interpretation once identified.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: That the intended target is the obvious one. Target assessment is a longitude and geometry problem and the answer is frequently not what the first look suggests.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Not applicable to the interceptor. The observable is a breakup on the target.

confusable_with.class: Orbital insertion or a sounding rocket
confusable_with.discriminator: A transfer orbit circularises at apogee. A ballistic profile does not and returns.

archetypes.name: Missile early warning platform
archetypes.built_to: Detect and track missile launches using infrared sensors, from geosynchronous or highly elliptical orbits.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Stationary at a longitude giving coverage of a region of interest, or in a highly elliptical orbit dwelling over high latitudes. Very stable, with routine station-keeping only.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Extremely regular. Manoeuvres are station-keeping and follow a cadence. Any departure from that cadence is notable precisely because the baseline is so consistent.
can: Provide strategic warning
Cue other systems
cannot: Manoeuvre aggressively without giving up its coverage, which makes it a predictable and therefore vulnerable object
archetypes.presence_implies: A high-value asset whose position is known to everyone. Objects that approach it are of immediate interest.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Very stable curve, consistent with a three-axis stabilised platform holding a fixed attitude.

confusable_with.discriminator: Both are stable at a longitude. Constellation membership and coverage geometry distinguish them, and this is a case where publicly available information does more work than observation.

archetypes.name: Signals intelligence platform with deployable antenna
archetypes.built_to: Collect radio-frequency emissions across a wide area using a large deployable mesh antenna.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Geosynchronous, stable, positioned for coverage of a region. The deployment of the antenna after launch is itself an observable event.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Stable once deployed. Photometric signature is distinctive because a large mesh antenna reflects differently from a compact bus.
can: Collect over a very wide area continuously
Change coverage only by relocating, which is slow and visible
cannot: Collect selectively against a single close target the way a proximity collector can
archetypes.presence_implies: Wide-area collection over whatever region it covers. The coverage footprint matters more than the object's immediate neighbours.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: Interest in any particular nearby object.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Distinctive, often bright for its size, with a step change at antenna deployment. A useful case where photometry says something about configuration that orbital data cannot.

confusable_with.discriminator: Both may carry large antennas. Publicly available information on the programme is usually the discriminator rather than any observable.

archetypes.name: Imaging platform
archetypes.built_to: Collect optical, infrared or radar imagery of the Earth's surface, usually from low Earth orbit.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Sun-synchronous or near-polar, in a plane chosen for revisit and lighting. Manoeuvres are altitude maintenance and occasional plane adjustment.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Highly regular. Frequently part of a constellation with tightly managed plane spacing, which is why plane matching against such a constellation is so visible.
can: Image a target repeatedly at a fixed local time
Manoeuvre to adjust revisit
cannot: Loiter over a target, being in low orbit and moving quickly
archetypes.presence_implies: Surface imaging in a known band. Where a foreign object plane matches such a constellation, the question is whether it wants to observe the constellation or use its plane.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Regular, with variation from body-pointing during collection.

confusable_with.discriminator: Radar imagers are typically in different planes and have distinctive large antenna structures. Radio-frequency observation distinguishes them where optical cannot.

archetypes.name: Communications relay
archetypes.built_to: Relay signals between ground stations, or between other satellites and the ground.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Geosynchronous, held tightly at a registered longitude slot, with routine north-south and east-west station-keeping.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: The most predictable class in the belt. Regular station-keeping on a known cadence, with north-south control consuming the large majority of the fuel budget.
can: Relay across a wide footprint
Be relocated slowly if the operator chooses
cannot: Manoeuvre rapidly or evade without losing service
archetypes.presence_implies: Usually nothing in itself. This class matters because it is what other things are interested in.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: Anything adversarial, including where operated by a country of concern. Most are exactly what they appear to be.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Very stable, with predictable seasonal variation from solar array tracking.

confusable_with.discriminator: Frequently indistinguishable by observation alone, which is why publicly available information on the programme carries the assessment.

archetypes.name: Navigation platform
archetypes.built_to: Broadcast timing and positioning signals from medium Earth orbit.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Medium Earth orbit in a managed constellation with defined slots. Manoeuvres are slot maintenance and are infrequent.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Extremely stable. Retirement to a disposal orbit at end of life is a normal and observable event.
can: Provide positioning and timing over a wide area
cannot: Manoeuvre substantially without leaving its slot and degrading the constellation
archetypes.presence_implies: Little in itself. Relevant mainly because a derelict navigation satellite drifting in a disposal orbit is a plausible target for a servicing or capture demonstration.

confusable_with.discriminator: An active platform maintains its slot. A derelict drifts and may tumble, and the photometry says which.

archetypes.name: Upper stage or transfer vehicle
archetypes.built_to: Deliver a payload to its operational orbit, then be discarded.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Present after a launch, frequently in a transfer orbit, and often tumbling once spent. Large radar cross-section relative to its brightness.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: No manoeuvres after payload delivery. Tumbling is normal and produces a periodic photometric signature. May shed debris as it ages.
can: Deliver a payload across a large altitude change
Perform multiple burns before disposal
cannot: Manoeuvre after disposal, which is what makes a manoeuvring apparent upper stage so interesting
archetypes.presence_implies: A recent launch, and an object that will be in the catalogue for a long time.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: Threat. But an object catalogued as an upper stage that manoeuvres has been mis-catalogued or is not what it appears, and that is a genuine finding.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Periodic variation from tumbling, often with a clear rotation period.

confusable_with.discriminator: Manoeuvre capability. Also tumbling: a controlled payload holds attitude and an upper stage usually does not.

archetypes.name: Reusable spaceplane
archetypes.built_to: Operate on orbit for an extended period carrying payloads, then return to a runway landing.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Low Earth orbit with substantial manoeuvre capability and no evident fuel constraint over the mission. May deploy and later recover sub-satellites.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Wide-ranging orbital changes across a long mission. Deployment of small objects that station-keep nearby is a recorded behaviour, as is subsequent close approach activity with them.
can: Change orbit substantially and repeatedly
Deploy objects and potentially recover them
Return to Earth with whatever it is carrying
cannot: Reach high orbits
Be assumed to have a fixed configuration between missions
archetypes.presence_implies: Flexibility rather than a specific mission. From a threat perspective all options are open, which is precisely what makes it hard to assess.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: Any single mission. Its payload may differ from flight to flight.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Variable, since configuration may change during the mission.

confusable_with.discriminator: Eventual deorbit and controlled landing, and the breadth of orbital change during the mission.

archetypes.name: Derelict or failed object
archetypes.orbital_signature: Drifts without control. In the belt, drifts through the graveyard region or through the operational belt depending on where it failed. Tumbles.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: No manoeuvres. Drift rate is determined by where it stopped. Sheds debris as material degrades.
can: Nothing deliberate
cannot: Manoeuvre, avoid, or be tasked
archetypes.presence_implies: A hazard and, increasingly, a target of interest for servicing and capture demonstrations.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: That it is safe to ignore. A derelict drifting through the operational belt is a conjunction problem for everyone it passes.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Periodic tumbling signature, frequently with a slowly changing rotation period.

confusable_with.discriminator: A derelict cannot correct its drift. Watch across enough time and the absence of correction is definitive.

archetypes.name: Technology demonstrator
archetypes.built_to: Test something. What it is testing is often not publicly stated and may not be evident from behaviour.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Variable by definition. Frequently exhibits behaviour that does not fit any other archetype, which is the point.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Unpredictable and worth watching for that reason alone. Behaviour that does not fit an established pattern is the class marker.
can: Almost anything, since the class exists to try things
cannot: Be assessed confidently from behaviour alone
archetypes.presence_implies: That an established pattern of life may not exist yet, and that early behaviour is establishing rather than departing from a baseline.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: Threat, though a demonstrator proving a capability is the normal precursor to that capability being fielded.

confusable_with.discriminator: This is the residual class. Assigning an object to it should be a considered judgement rather than a default when nothing else fits, and the honest report says a pattern of life is not yet established.

archetypes.name: Small satellite constellation member
archetypes.built_to: Operate as one of many near-identical objects providing a service through numbers rather than individual capability.
archetypes.orbital_signature: Low Earth orbit in a managed shell with tight plane and phase spacing. Frequent small automated manoeuvres for collision avoidance and constellation maintenance.
archetypes.typical_behaviour: Very high manoeuvre rate across the constellation, overwhelmingly automated and routine. Individual manoeuvres are almost never significant.
can: Provide service through redundancy
Manoeuvre automatically and frequently
cannot: Do much individually, which is why individual members rarely warrant attention
archetypes.presence_implies: Background. The analytically interesting question is when something else plane matches the shell.
archetypes.presence_does_not_imply: That any individual manoeuvre means anything. Treating constellation manoeuvres as events would swamp any cell.
archetypes.photometric_expectation: Consistent across members, which makes an outlier within a constellation genuinely notable.

confusable_with.class: A foreign object hiding within a constellation shell
confusable_with.discriminator: Consistency. A member that behaves or looks unlike its siblings is worth a second look, and this is the strongest argument for knowing what normal looks like across a class.

reasoning_rules.note: How to use the archetypes analytically rather than as labels.
rules: Reason from behaviour to class, then from class to meaning. Never from name to conclusion.
The cannot list does more work than the can list, because it eliminates hypotheses. An object that manoeuvres is not a derelict, whatever the catalogue says.
Where two classes share an observable, say so. Servicing and co-orbital attack share an approach profile, and no geometry distinguishes them. Report capability and observation separately from intent.
A platform class supplies a prior, not an answer. It tells you what is likely, and the evidence tells you what happened.
Where an object fits no class, say that rather than forcing it into the residual class. A pattern of life that does not yet exist is a finding.
The mission paragraph in a report is where this knowledge appears. It is hedged, sourced from public information, and kept separate from the observational assessment.
